Exact Title: Mapping the Landscape of Software Vulnerabilities in Connected Vehicles
Authors: Srijita Basu, Miroslaw Staron, Magnus Almgren, Jennifer Horkoff, Christian Berger
Research Objective & RQs: Analyze attack vectors, SDLC phases, and vulnerabilities in modern Connected Vehicles (CVs); investigate if automotive flaws shifted from physical ECUs to cloud/apps.
Dataset & Sample Size: 413 CV vulnerabilities (2022-2024), 20 repositories containing 827 vulnerable libraries, 7-year historical CV vulnerability database (1,507 unique CVEs).
Methodology & Evaluation: Empirical analysis of NVD/GitHub CV advisories; mapping across SDLC phases (Design, Coding, Testing, Deployment), CAPEC attack vectors, and CWE categories.
Baselines & Metrics: Descriptive trend comparisons across 7 years; CVSS v3 severity distribution, attack surface proportions.
Main Findings (Author Terminology): Proportion of CV vulnerabilities in external apps/cloud services tripled compared to physical ECUs; basic weaknesses (default credentials, unauthenticated endpoints) remain pervasive; privacy risks outpace physical manipulation.
Author-Stated Limitations: Data limited to publicly disclosed vulnerabilities; GitHub repository scanning relied on open-source automotive repos which may not reflect proprietary OEM codebases.
Critical Assessment Limitations: Lacks component-level package URL (purl) or CPE identifiers; vendor labels are coarse text strings; does not evaluate transitive supply-chain dependency trees or regulatory assurance claims.
AutoSupplyGuard Component Enabled: Layer 1 (Vulnerability Ingestion) and Layer 3 (Vulnerability Correlation Engine) for automotive-specific CVE benchmark.
Unsupported Claims:
Does NOT prove which specific vehicle models or production supplier tiers actually deployed the vulnerable libraries; does not prove exploitability in a closed vehicular CAN bus.

Exact Title: A Dataset of Software Bill of Materials for Evaluating SBOM Consumption Tools
Research Objective & RQs: Provide a curated benchmark of validated SBOMs with ground truth data sources to evaluate SBOM consumption, parsing, and dependency tools.
Dataset & Sample Size: 46 curated open-source projects; 46 SPDX-2.2 JSON documents with 995 packages and 995 explicit dependency relationships.
Methodology & Evaluation: Curated extraction from active projects with companion data-source manifests documenting package repositories and commit revisions.
Baselines & Metrics: Ground truth package and relationship recovery rate (precision/recall).
Main Findings (Author Terminology): Demonstrates that even standardized SPDX documents exhibit subtle variation in package ID conventions and relationship types across different generators.
Author-Stated Limitations: Small sample size (46 projects); focus on open-source general-purpose software rather than embedded systems or automotive ECUs.
Critical Assessment Limitations: Does not include CycloneDX documents or automotive embedded firmware SBOMs; small sample limits statistical generalization.
AutoSupplyGuard Component Enabled: Layer 2 (Normalisation) and Layer 5 (Dependency Graph) benchmark for exact ground truth verification of package and dependency extraction.
Unsupported Claims: Cannot be used as proof of automotive supply chain coverage or multi-tier supplier compliance.

Exact Title: Security Assurance Cases for Road Vehicles: An Industry Perspective
Authors: Mazen Mohamad, Alexander Åström, Örjan Askerdal, Jörgen Borg, Riccardo Scandariato
Venue / Identifier: 15th International Conference on Availability, Reliability and Security (ARES 2020), arXiv:2003.14106
Research Objective & RQs: Investigate industrial challenges and practical requirements for developing Security Assurance Cases (SACs) in automotive road vehicles aligned with ISO/SAE 21434.
Dataset & Sample Size: Empirical study with two major Swedish automotive OEMs (Volvo Group and Volvo Cars) involving 14 senior engineers and managers.
Methodology & Evaluation: Qualitative and semi-structured empirical interview study; thematic coding of industrial engineering practices and compliance requirements.
Baselines & Metrics: Comparison of functional safety assurance (ISO 26262) vs. security assurance (ISO/SAE 21434) workflows.
Main Findings (Author Terminology): Automotive organizations struggle to connect low-level engineering artifacts to high-level security claims; security assurance requires dynamic evidence maintenance due to post-deployment vulnerability emergence; lack of traceability between component suppliers and OEM assurance cases.
Author-Stated Limitations: Qualitative study based on Swedish automotive context; findings represent perceived challenges rather than an automated technical framework.
Critical Assessment Limitations: Does not provide a concrete software implementation or machine-readable graph schema for automated claim evaluation.
AutoSupplyGuard Component Enabled: Layer 4 (Traceability Graph) and Layer 5 (Assurance Engine) — directly shapes AutoSupplyGuard claim-evidence schema and freshness/staleness rules.
Unsupported Claims: Does not define an executable algorithm for automated evidence checking; does not provide an empirical component database.
